 Southeast Asia’s banks face scrutiny over financing of haze-linked companies
 The region’s biggest banks continue to finance plantation firms linked to Indonesian forest fires, exposing gaps in green lending pledges and environmental safeguards.
 November 16, 2026 | Written by Robin Hicks 
 Photo by Ulet Ifansasti for Greenpeace Indonesia / Flickr.
 Key points:
 Southeast Asia’s major banks continue financing plantation companies linked to Indonesian forest fires, despite adopting no-deforestation and no-peat policies. 
 Central banks have urged lenders to assess environmental risks, but voluntary guidelines and weak disclosure requirements leave significant gaps in tackling haze-linked financing. 
 Greater scrutiny of banks’ lending practices, due diligence and exposure to fire-prone concessions could offer a new way to hold financiers accountable for the haze. 
 Southeast Asia’s largest banks are facing growing scrutiny over their financing of companies linked to transboundary air pollution from burning Indonesian peatlands.
 Gaps in banks’ environmental and social safeguards have been identified in lending to plantation firms whose concessions have burned during the region’s worst haze outbreak in more than a decade. 
 Supercharged by an El Niño-fuelled dry season, the 2026 fires have caused more than 330,000 respiratory illnesses in Indonesia, forced schools to close in Malaysia and are projected to cost Singapore’s economy up to US$3bn. 
 More than 1.92m hectares (4.8bn acres) burned across Indonesia by September, with a quarter of the fires occurring inside company concessions, according to Nusantara Atlas , which tracks the activity of palm oil and mining companies. 
 In an unprecedented speech on 19 October, Singaporean minister K Shanmugam named the palm oil and paper companies linked to the fires and highlighted the role of banks in properly managing haze risk. Singapore’s stated intention to pursue companies responsible for the fires briefly sent palm oil stocks tumbling . 
 Most of the region’s major banks have adopted no deforestation, no peatland development and no exploitation (NDPE) policies intended to restrict lending to problematic companies. But these commitments have not stopped money flowing to businesses with fire-affected concessions. 
 An October study by the non-profit coalition Forests & Finance found that companies named by Shanmugam and in a   Greenpeace report have received billions in financing from the region’s leading banks. 
 Indonesian conglomerate Sinar Mas, owner of paper giant Asia Pulp & Paper (APP), received more financing ($62.4bn in total) than any other agricultural company in Southeast Asia over the past decade, the study found. 
 APP supplier concessions have burned this year, prompting administrative sanctions by the Indonesian government and an investigation by Singapore’s National Environment Agency. APP made a zero-burning pledge across its supply chain in 1997 and adopted an NDPE policy in 2013. 
 “The missing piece” in bank lending policies is a rigorous assessment of haze risk and fire vulnerability, says Stephanie Dowlen, senior finance campaigner at Rainforest Action Network, which co-produced the Forests & Finance report. 
 “Banks tell their clients they are not allowed to intentionally light fires to clear land – but that’s not the key issue,” she says. “It’s that they are developing on peat and running production models that degrade the land into a tinderbox.” 
 Voluntary NDPE pledges and sustainability certifications such as those of the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oi l have failed to guarantee haze-free production, Dowlen says, partly because violations do not trigger sufficiently timely or serious penalties. 
 How central banks are responding 
 The Association of Banks in Singapore issued guidelines in 2015 urging lenders to avoid financing companies linked to haze. But its haze diagnostics kit, part of its Responsible Finance Guidelines , remains voluntary. 
 Singapore’s central bank, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), said on 28 October that it expects banks to identify material environmental risks from lending to agribusinesses and obtain information from clients linked to the haze. This includes whether they have taken adequate steps to prevent, detect and stop fires. 
 MAS said these expectations were set out in its 2020 Guidelines on Environmental Risk Management and reinforced by its Guidelines on Transition Planning , issued in March. 
 Malaysia’s central bank, Bank Negara Malaysia, told Green Central Banking that banks should use the country’s climate change and principle-based taxonomy to assess lending risks. Financial institutions are expected to conduct due diligence and manage material environmental risks, it said, adding that it takes a “proportionate and risk-based approach” to supervision. 
 Indonesia’s financial regulator, Otoritas Jasa Keuangan, did not respond to questions. But in a   September statement , it warned that fires posed a direct risk to the banking sector by threatening borrowers’ ability to meet debt obligations. 
 Indonesian banks are the biggest lenders to Southeast Asia’s haze-risk companies, led by Bank Central Asia, Bank Mandiri and Bank Negara Indonesia. They have NDPE commitments and exclusion lists, and are subject to sustainable finance regulations and the country’s green finance taxonomy. 
 But these measures fall short of binding limits on financing companies linked to fires, says Linda Rosalina, executive director of Tuk Indonesia, an environmental and human rights organisation. In July, Tuk called on Indonesian banks to strengthen due diligence on plantation companies ahead of an El Niño year. It is also considering suing banks that persistently finance companies linked to forest fires, Rosalina says. 
 Data gaps 
 Malaysian, Singaporean and Japanese banks are also major funders of companies operating on Indonesian peatlands. 
 First Resources, a palm oil producer named by Greenpeace among the companies most affected by fires, received $450m in credit from Japan’s SMBC, Singapore’s UOB and DBS, and Malaysia’s Maybank between 2021 and 2026, according to Forests & Finance. 
 But establishing whether banks’ safeguards are working is difficult, says Holly Yang, professor of accounting at Singapore Management University (SMU). 
 Banks rely on information from borrowers, whose ownership structures, concession boundaries and supply chains can be difficult to trace. Indonesian concession boundaries are often fragmented across permits and corporate entities, while overlapping land claims and inconsistent public records complicate efforts to establish responsibility for individual areas. 
 The use of shadow companies by large plantation and pulpwood groups in Indonesia, such as Royal Golden Eagle , APP and First Resources , further obscures corporate responsibility. 
 Although banks disclose their sector exposure and environmental, social and governance assessment processes, it is difficult to establish how much lending is linked to fire-affected concessions, what corrective action borrowers take and whether it prevents further fires, Yang says. 
 More detailed reporting by banks on their exposure and how they monitor clients would help investors assess whether safeguards are reducing haze risk, she says. 
 Yang and her SMU colleagues have mapped companies with the most fire-affected concessions and their lenders in a flow chart to illustrate the connections. 
 Haze and finance flow chart by SMU. 
 Legal leverage 
 A more effective way to tackle haze financing may be to shift the legal focus from who started an individual fire to who finances businesses that create the conditions for fires. 
 Proving responsibility for specific fires – and linking their health impacts to particular companies – is difficult, says Kuala Lumpur-based environmental lawyer Kiu Jia Yaw. This has limited the effectiveness of existing laws. 
 Singapore’s Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, enacted in 2014, allows action against entities whose conduct causes or contributes to haze pollution in Singapore, including through activities overseas. But more than a decade after the 2015 haze, investigations into four APP companies remain open , with no known prosecutions or fines under the law. 
 July versus September haze. Image by CREA. 
 Instead, regulators could scrutinise whether lenders adequately assess and manage the environmental risks associated with their clients’ operations, Kiu says. 
 A plantation operating on drained peatland, for example, may pose a significant fire risk if it fails to maintain safe water levels. Banks should examine such practices before extending credit and require borrowers to address deficiencies. 
 This would not automatically make lenders legally liable for fires, but could pressure them to withdraw financing from companies that repeatedly fail to manage foreseeable environmental risks, he says. 
 Regulators could reinforce this by requiring banks to disclose their exposure to fire-prone concessions, the environmental checks they conduct and the action they take when clients fall short. 
 Kiu points to Malaysia’s National Sustainability Reporting Framework , which adopts international sustainability disclosure standards, as a possible foundation for more consistent reporting. 
 He also suggests extending the approach across Southeast Asia through a protocol to the 2002 Asean Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution . Such a protocol could establish common standards for assessing and disclosing haze-related financial risks, he says. 
 Ultimately, financial institutions have a fiduciary duty to ensure capital does not support businesses contributing to haze risk, and should be mindful that funding plundered peatlands is not environmentally – or financially – sustainable, Kiu cautions. 
 “The plantation companies will eventually reap what they sow. If they maintain production models that are degenerative, there will be no long-term payback.”

 Written by
 Robin Hicks 
 Robin Hicks is a Singapore-based journalist covering nature, climate and business in Asia. Robin has written for Green Central Banking since 2026. He also writes for Mongabay, Dialogue Earth, Reuters, ImpactAlpha and Jom. On weekends, he volunteers for wildlife rescue charity ACRES.
